spec.description: How the Internet's data centres are joined: some 4,200 data centres from PeeringDB, sized by the networks in them, the world's submarine cables, and the latest round trip from about 1,000 RIPE Atlas anchors to the one picked; reloaded every 5 minutes.

options.content:
### Where the data comes from

Three open registers of how the Internet's data centres are joined, read with no key:

- **[PeeringDB](https://www.peeringdb.com/)**: the register networks keep of where they interconnect. Each data centre (a *facility*) with its operator, its place, and how many networks (ASNs), exchanges and carriers say they are in it. Only those with a place and at least one network show. Kept by the networks themselves, so a building is as complete as its tenants made it.
- **[Submarine Cable Map](https://www.submarinecablemap.com/)** by TeleGeography: the routes of the cables under the sea, and where they come ashore. The routes are drawn to show where a cable runs, not its exact track.
- **[RIPE Atlas](https://atlas.ripe.net/)**: some 1,100 *anchors*, measuring servers hosted in data centres and networks around the world. Each anchor is pinged by all the others every four minutes (the *anchoring mesh*); the map shows the latest round of that mesh for the anchor picked in **Ping to**.

### How to read it

- A dot is an anchor, and an arc one of the nearest anchors pinging the target (**Arcs from** sets how many): the colour is the mean round trip of three packets, green under 30 ms, then yellow-green to 80, yellow to 150, orange to 250 and red beyond. Its comets run faster the shorter the trip. An anchor whose packets were all lost does not show, and counts in **Lost**.
- A round trip is there and back, so a one-way delay is about half of it. Light in fibre covers some 100 km per millisecond of round trip, so a trip well above what the distance asks for means a long route, not a slow link: between two neighbours in Latin America, traffic can still go by way of Miami.
- The data centres, in violet, are sized by the networks in them: the big dots are where networks meet, and where traffic between them stays local. **Region** picks the data centres the table lists; the map shows all of them.

### How it works

Grafana's DuckDB reads the registers through the stack's gateway, which keeps PeeringDB, the cables and the list of anchors a day, and the latest pings four minutes, the mesh's own interval: each source is asked once whoever is looking, and PeeringDB, which lets an anonymous reader have its whole list once an hour, is never asked twice. DuckDB running in your browser (the Chaski data source) then answers every panel. The map is the Kepler Geospatial Maps Plus panel, with its Traffic layer for the pings and its Pipeline layer for the cables. The dashboard reloads every five minutes.

spec.rawSql: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE rtt_ms IS NOT NULL) AS "Answering" FROM $latency

spec.description: Anchors whose latest ping to the target had at least one packet back.
spec.title: Answering

spec.description: Cables on the Submarine Cable Map, in service or planned.
spec.title: Cables

spec.rawSql:
SELECT country AS "Country", median(rtt_ms) AS "Round trip"
FROM $latency WHERE rtt_ms IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY country
QUALIFY row_number() OVER (ORDER BY count(*) DESC) <= 30
ORDER BY "Round trip"

spec.description: The median of the latest round trips from the anchors of each country, the nearest first: the 30 countries with the most anchors answering.
spec.title: Median round trip to ${target:text}, by country

spec.rawSql:
SELECT name AS "Data centre", city || ', ' || country AS "City",
       networks AS "Networks", exchanges AS "IXPs"
FROM $facilities WHERE ('${region:raw}' = 'World' OR region = '${region:raw}')
ORDER BY networks DESC LIMIT 200

spec.description: Where networks meet: the data centres of the region picked, by how many networks (ASNs) say they are in them, and how many Internet exchanges (IXPs) are there.
spec.title: Data centres in ${region:raw}, most networks first

spec.rawSql: SELECT count(*) AS "Data centres" FROM $facilities WHERE ('${region:raw}' = 'World' OR region = '${region:raw}')

spec.description: Data centres in PeeringDB, in the region picked, with a place and at least one network.
spec.title: Data centres

spec.rawSql:
SELECT source AS "From", company || ' (AS' || asn || ')' AS "Hosted by", rtt_ms AS "Round trip"
FROM $latency WHERE rtt_ms IS NOT NULL ORDER BY rtt_ms LIMIT 50

spec.description: The anchors with the shortest latest round trip to the target: their place, who hosts them and in which network (ASN), and the mean round trip of three packets.
spec.title: Nearest anchors to ${target:text}

spec.description: The share of all the packets of the latest round that never came back.
spec.title: Lost

spec.rawSql:
-- Every submarine cable, along its route.
SELECT cable, name, geometry AS geom FROM $cables

-- Where the cables come ashore.
SELECT name, latitude, longitude FROM $landings

-- Every data centre with a network in it, the busiest drawn last, on top.
SELECT name, operator, city, country, networks, exchanges, carriers, latitude, longitude
FROM $facilities ORDER BY networks

-- A dot for every anchor that answered, the slowest drawn first.
SELECT source, company, asn, rtt_ms, loss_pct, time, srclat, srclng
FROM $latency WHERE rtt_ms IS NOT NULL ORDER BY rtt_ms DESC

-- The target itself.
SELECT DISTINCT target, target_company, dstlat AS latitude, dstlng AS longitude FROM $latency

spec.description: Every data centre in PeeringDB with a network in it, sized by how many (violet); the submarine cables and where they come ashore (blue); and every RIPE Atlas anchor, coloured by its latest round trip to the one picked in Ping to, green under 30 ms to red over 250, with an arc from the nearest (Arcs from). Hover a dot or an arc for its details.
spec.title: Data centres, submarine cables and round trips to ${target:text}

spec.description: The median round trip time (RTT): the median of the latest mean round trips from every anchor that answered to the target.
spec.title: Median RTT

spec.description: The shortest of the latest round trips to the target, from another anchor.
spec.title: Fastest

spec.description: The RIPE Atlas anchor that the other anchors ping: an always-on measuring server hosted in a data centre or a network.
spec.label: Ping to
spec.name: target

spec.__legacyStringValue:
-- Every RIPE Atlas anchor that others ping (its mesh measurement), by place
-- and host; the anchors in Ecuador first. Lists cached a day by the gateway.
WITH anchors AS (
  SELECT a.fqdn, a.city, a.country, a.company
  FROM (SELECT unnest(results) AS a FROM read_json(['http://feeds/atlas/anchors/1.json', 'http://feeds/atlas/anchors/2.json', 'http://feeds/atlas/anchors/3.json'], maximum_object_size = 100000000))
),
mesh AS (
  SELECT m.id, m.target FROM (SELECT unnest(results) AS m FROM read_json(['http://feeds/atlas/mesh/1.json', 'http://feeds/atlas/mesh/2.json', 'http://feeds/atlas/mesh/3.json'], maximum_object_size = 100000000))
)
SELECT a.city || ', ' || a.country || ' · ' || a.company AS __text, CAST(m.id AS VARCHAR) AS __value
FROM mesh m JOIN anchors a ON a.fqdn = m.target
ORDER BY a.country = 'EC' DESC, __text

spec.description: How many anchors draw an arc to the target, the nearest first. Every anchor that answered is a dot.
spec.label: Arcs from
spec.name: arcs

query.rawSql:
-- Server side: every data centre in PeeringDB with a place and at least one
-- network in it, through the gateway, which asks PeeringDB once a day (see
-- gateway/feeds.conf). net_count is the networks (ASNs) present in the
-- building, ix_count the exchanges, carrier_count the carriers.
SELECT f.id, f.name, f.org_name AS operator, f.city, f.country,
       coalesce(f.region_continent, 'Unknown') AS region,
       f.latitude, f.longitude, f.net_count AS networks, f.ix_count AS exchanges,
       f.carrier_count AS carriers
FROM (SELECT unnest(data) AS f FROM read_json('http://feeds/peeringdb/fac', maximum_object_size = 100000000))
WHERE f.latitude IS NOT NULL AND f.longitude IS NOT NULL AND f.net_count > 0

-- Server side: every submarine cable on TeleGeography's map, its route as
-- GeoJSON, through the gateway, which keeps it a day.
SELECT f.properties.id AS cable, f.properties.name AS name,
       to_json(f.geometry)::VARCHAR AS geometry
FROM (SELECT unnest(features) AS f FROM read_json('http://feeds/cables/cable.json', maximum_object_size = 100000000))

-- Server side: where the submarine cables come ashore.
SELECT f.properties.id AS id, f.properties.name AS name,
       f.geometry.coordinates[2] AS latitude, f.geometry.coordinates[1] AS longitude
FROM (SELECT unnest(features) AS f FROM read_json('http://feeds/cables/landing-point.json', maximum_object_size = 100000000))

spec.label: Pings to the target anchor (one row per anchor)
spec.name: latency

query.rawSql:
-- Server side: the latest ping from every RIPE Atlas anchor to the one picked
-- ($target, its mesh measurement), three packets every four minutes, through
-- the gateway, which keeps the results four minutes. Each row is a link from
-- the anchor that pinged to the target: rtt_ms is the mean round trip, null
-- when no packet came back.
WITH anchors AS (
  SELECT a.probe, a.fqdn, a.city, a.country, a.company, a.as_v4::BIGINT AS asn,
         a.geometry.coordinates[2] AS latitude, a.geometry.coordinates[1] AS longitude
  FROM (SELECT unnest(results) AS a FROM read_json(['http://feeds/atlas/anchors/1.json', 'http://feeds/atlas/anchors/2.json', 'http://feeds/atlas/anchors/3.json'], maximum_object_size = 100000000))
),
mesh AS (
  SELECT m.id, m.target FROM (SELECT unnest(results) AS m FROM read_json(['http://feeds/atlas/mesh/1.json', 'http://feeds/atlas/mesh/2.json', 'http://feeds/atlas/mesh/3.json'], maximum_object_size = 100000000))
),
target AS (SELECT a.* FROM mesh m JOIN anchors a ON a.fqdn = m.target WHERE m.id = ${target:raw}),
latest AS (
  SELECT prb_id, avg, min, sent, rcvd, to_timestamp(timestamp) AS time
  FROM read_json('http://feeds/atlas/latest/${target:raw}.json', maximum_object_size = 100000000,
                 columns = {prb_id: 'BIGINT', avg: 'DOUBLE', min: 'DOUBLE', sent: 'INTEGER', rcvd: 'INTEGER', timestamp: 'BIGINT'})
)
SELECT s.fqdn AS anchor, s.city || ', ' || s.country AS source, s.country, s.company, s.asn,
       s.latitude AS srclat, s.longitude AS srclng,
       t.city || ', ' || t.country AS target, t.company AS target_company,
       t.latitude AS dstlat, t.longitude AS dstlng,
       CASE WHEN l.avg > 0 THEN round(l.avg, 1) END AS rtt_ms,
       CASE WHEN l.min > 0 THEN round(l.min, 1) END AS rtt_min_ms,
       round(100.0 * (l.sent - l.rcvd) / nullif(l.sent, 0))::INTEGER AS loss_pct,
       -- Comets run faster on a shorter round trip.
       CASE WHEN l.avg > 0 THEN round(least(20, 400 / l.avg), 2) END AS pace,
       l.time
FROM latest l JOIN anchors s ON s.probe = l.prb_id CROSS JOIN target t
WHERE s.latitude IS NOT NULL AND s.fqdn <> t.fqdn
